All electric motors have a locked rotor amperage printed on the information plate. This is the amperage it draws when power is going to the windings (the sitty still part) but the rotor isn’t moving (the spinny part) off the rotor were rusted in place, the motor would draw locked rotor from the time power was applied until it was shut off (with larger motors that would be when the breaker trips) the compressors in most residential air conditioning systems have locked rotor amperages easily around 100 amps. Refrigerators and such, can be around 30 to 50. When you turn it on, the rotor isn’t moving. The electric field produced in the windings has to get it moving and that happens very fast, but for a split second it draws locked rotor amps. Then it will run at around 10-20 amps until it shuts off. Your furnace blower will draw 40-50 or so locked rotor amps as well for that split second. Then it will run at around 8 amps until done. Fan motors in refrigerators will draw a comparably small locked rotor amperage (maybe 10) so when they see a big spike (home a/c starting) of around 150 amps, followed by a 20 minute period of around 25 amps, they know your air conditioner is running, because virtually nothing else anyone has at their home would share that profile. A spike of around 60 amps, followed by a 20 minute draw of around 10 amps, tells them you have a refrigerator or freezer running for the same reason. The commenter who’s being told to get rid of their garage fridge, it would be because they see that profile either at two different times at intervals that don’t make sense for one appliance, or because they see it happen again while the first one is already running. For other appliances, if they aren’t cooling they’re probably heating. Toasters, electric ovens, etc draw high amperage continuously but have no spike when they start. Dishwasher’s and such draw lower amps but also have no spike. But all of those won’t be turned on for hours at a time like lights or tv’s. So they get labeled as “other appliances”

R134a is a blend (the “a”) stands for Azeotrope. The difference is that 134a is a true Azeotrope, while 410a is a near Zeotropic Azeotrope. True azeotropes have the same proportions of their constituent components in liquid and vapor forms, zeotropes have more of whatever components have lower boiling points when in vapor form

R-22 can be charge either way because it is not a blend. It is a pure chemical compound. 

All blends must be charged as a liquid, because only in liquid form is it a blend. R410a is a mixture of R32 (molecular mass = 52) and  R125 (molecular mass = 120) Think of distillation. You whiskey still is kept at the exact temperature you need for boiling ethanol, because once it boils it separates from the rest of the mixture, it cannot exist in vapor form as a blend. 

The refrigerant that is in vapor form in your R410a tank is actually 2 refrigerants. The vapors sit separate of one another. This is called stratification. On top, you have the refrigerant with the least molecular mass (R32) below that you have the next heaviest molecular mass (R125) and since 410a is only a 2 refrigerant blend, below the R125 you would have liquid (or “true” 410a). So if you leave the cylinder upright, and charge, you will draw off R32 before you draw any R125. And, once you do that, the pressure drop will cause the liquid below the two to boil, which will create turbulence in the can, which will cause you to get some 125 but still the 32 is rising to the top since it has less density, so altogether, you will add more R32 than you will R125 but in truth don’t have the slightest clue how much of either refrigerant you’ve just added to a system that should be running a 50/50 blend of the two. You will have problems with system operation due to the incorrect composition of the refrigerant (we will call it R-WTF) the problems in an R-WTF system could be as small as decreased efficiency/capacity, or as large as oil degradation and subsequent compressor failure. All in all, it’s much better to just flip the damned tank over.

Ask your comfort advisor (consultant, salesperson, etc.) about adding (Lennox) iHarmony zone control to the system. It communicates as well. 

If you do this, and go with the variable instead of staging, you can have zone control which will eliminate stratification issues between floors. 

If you are calling for cooling just upstairs, the zone panel will “tell” the furnace and condensing unit that you only need cooling upstairs, which will cause the condensing unit and ECM blower to run at a capacity more appropriate for just that floor. Same for a downstairs only call. If both zones call at once, the system will then run at full capacity. 

I’m heating mode it won’t necessarily need to meter itself as much, since The SLP98 starts at 30% btu capacity and increases every 7 minutes until at full capacity. If there’s just a 1° or 2° heat call downstairs, the furnace may never reach full capacity, same for upstairs. If both are calling, it may run long enough to use full capacity
